title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) that tested whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task, reused across both arms) and allowed up to one validator‑triggered repair in the guarded arm. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) using the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. All archived per‑task verdicts reported safe outcomes in both arms (baseline: 240/240 safe; guarded: 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could change an outcome only if the single shared candidate failed validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run every shared candidate passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, the verified numeric outcomes, an explicit difficulty composition of the task pool, and a failure analysis that explains the null paired result and provides concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe, multi‑device network configuration is a key NetOps challenge. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can synthesize candidate configurations and plans, but textual fidelity does not guarantee ordering, dependency, and invariant preservation required for safe application in live networks. Emulation‑grounded, closed‑loop evaluation surfaces semantic failures (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that static, text‑only tests miss [1].

Generate–validate–repair (GVR) architectures—LLM generation followed by deterministic validation and automated repair—are a recurring design pattern proposed to reduce unsafe actions in automated configuration pipelines [2], and related program/ configuration repair work documents success for many syntactic and localized semantic faults [3]. However, how much deterministic verification reduces unsafe applies in operationally realistic, distribution‑shifted, or adversarial settings remains an open empirical question that requires careful experimental control and preregistration.

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment that measured one precisely defined estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). The run adhered to the preregistered contract that used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (a single LLM generation per task reused across both arms) and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair in the guarded arm. Because of this contract, paired differences can arise only when the shared candidate fails deterministic validation or when a repair changes the final configuration. We preserve and cite archived execution and analysis artifacts that contain per‑task traces, validator verdicts, and the complete analysis outputs. Our contributions are (1) an artifact‑grounded execution and analysis of a preregistered paired GVR test; (2) explicit numeric accounting that maps the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs; and (3) a focused failure analysis explaining the observed null paired outcome and recommendations for future informative GVR designs.
sections.related_work: Executable, emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks place LLM agents into closed‑loop multi‑device networks and reveal failure modes beyond token errors; NetConfArena is one such benchmark [1]. Automatic configuration repair and program‑repair literature document generate–validate patterns and show that validators often enable high repair coverage on benchmarked faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design and fault model [2], [3]. Surveys of agentic LLM evaluation and NetOps/AIOps position papers emphasize tool augmentation, verifier integration, and workflow‑centred evaluation as necessary to assess operational reliability [4], [5]. Practical verifier engineering and incremental verification lessons are informed by configuration analysis tools such as Batfish [6]. Our study situates itself at the intersection of these lines by combining a preregistered paired estimand, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, deterministic emulation scoring, and full archival of per‑call and validator traces.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The primary analysis used a paired contingency estimator with bootstrap percentile 95% CI and an exact McNemar two‑sided test as preregistered.

Design and sampling: Paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation per task was produced and reused across both arms. N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks were blocked into topology/vendor clusters and composed as: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). The task generator produced intent payloads, initial states, required sequences, and constraints; tasks include difficulty labels recorded at generation time.

Model, oracle, and adapter contract: The declared model used in execution was gpt-5-mini. The deterministic validator used in the guarded pipeline implemented a finite set of semantic checks. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair; thus, the only mechanism for creating discordant paired outcomes is validator failure of the shared candidate and subsequent repair-induced change.

Scoring and exclusions: A deterministic emulator + validator assigned a binary final outcome per episode: safe (0) or unsafe (1) based on semantic invariant checks and simulated application. Preregistered exclusions included items flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator reports unsafe) and unrecoverable infra failures after allowed retries; such items would be handled in sensitivity analyses. The run followed the preregistered retry policy and exclusion rules.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed as planned with 240 complete pairs. The experiment consumed exactly one shared initial generation per task (one model call per task under the registered contract) and adhered to the adapter contract. No infrastructure failures or preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Observed counts: baseline safe = 240, baseline unsafe = 0; guarded safe = 240, guarded unsafe = 0. Paired contingency table: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed recorded in the archived analysis). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Difficulty composition: The archived task difficulty labels show two observed levels across the 240 tasks: 'very_hard' = 192 tasks (80.0%) and 'extreme' = 48 tasks (20.0%).

Validator activity and repairs: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in the guarded arm across the entire task set; repair invocation count = 0. Representative validator traces in the archive show validation verdicts and final_state snapshots for inspected tasks, and they confirm that the shared initial candidates passed the deterministic checks for all evaluated episodes. Because the shared initial candidate passed validation for every task, the guarded arm had no opportunity to alter final outcomes and the paired contrast is degenerate.

Unused sensitivity channels: The preregistered sensitivity analyses for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures were not exercised because no such items occurred; planned subgroup contrasts (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial) are numerically identical (all zeros) under the observed outcomes.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation of the null paired effect: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the experimental lever that could cause paired discordance was limited to validator failure of the single shared candidate (and subsequent repair). In this run, every shared candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs were invoked; therefore the guarded condition could not produce discordant outcomes and the paired estimator is necessarily zero. This mechanistic account is directly supported by the execution accounting and validator verdicts archived for each task.

Design implications and recommendations: To obtain an informative paired contrast that measures verifier causal contribution, future experiments should (A) use independent initial generations per arm (remove shared_initial_candidate semantics), (B) increase adversary strength or stochastic generator variability so validators have nontrivial failure opportunities, or (C) expand repair budgets (allow multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair traces to study repair search behavior. These design choices trade increased model call budgets for statistical informativeness; the precise choice should align with the estimand of interest (causal effect of validator vs operational benefit under fixed sampling budget).

Threats to validity: Internal validity is constrained by the chosen shared_initial_candidate contract, which was preregistered and adhered to; this contract limits causal interpretation to validator‑triggered changes of a single shared candidate. Construct validity depends on deterministic validator coverage; a finite check set may miss unmodeled semantic faults. External validity is limited by the synthetic emulation corpus and the single declared model tested; results do not generalize to all models, prompts, or production deployments. Conclusion validity is limited by the realized baseline unsafe rate of zero, which prevents detection of verifier benefit under the chosen contract.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration using shared_initial_candidate semantics and a deterministic validator. Observed outcome: all 240 pairs were safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract mechanically constrained the guarded arm’s ability to create discordant outcomes; because every shared initial candidate passed validation, no repairs were applied and the paired contrast was degenerate. Our artifact archive supports this account and suggests concrete, artifact‑grounded design changes (generation semantics, adversary strength, repair budget) that are necessary to produce informative paired contrasts in future studies.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: Execution used the declared hosted model "gpt-5-mini" via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration artifact recorded in the archive) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. Preregistered generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); therefore only validator failure of the shared candidate or a validator‑triggered repair could create paired differences. Immutable master prompt: the initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution artifacts (execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts) are archived and available for independent inspection. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic validator implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the validator.
